historic_environment_site_source: aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-history-historic-environment-sites-2026-2028 — site for Elizabethan England in the 2026 series is The Globe (officially confirmed by AQA, three-year advance notice).

lessons.title: Elizabeth I: background, character and the royal court
lessons.description: Who Elizabeth was in 1568, how she was raised and educated, and how the royal court actually worked.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — Elizabeth I and her court: background and character of Elizabeth I; court life, including patronage.

lessons.title: Key ministers: Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council
lessons.description: How William Cecil, Francis Walsingham and the Privy Council ran the country day to day for the queen.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — key ministers; court life, including patronage.

lessons.title: A female ruler: Parliament, marriage and the succession
lessons.description: Why Elizabeth's gender complicated everything from Parliament to the question of who would rule next.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — The difficulties of a female ruler: relations with Parliament; the problem of marriage and the succession.

lessons.title: Authority at the end of the reign and Essex's rebellion (1601)
lessons.description: How Elizabeth held on to power into old age, and why the Earl of Essex's rebellion in 1601 collapsed.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 1 — the strength of Elizabeth's authority at the end of her reign, including Essex's rebellion in 1601.

lessons.title: Religious matters: settlement, Catholics and Puritans
lessons.description: The Elizabethan religious settlement and the rival pressures from English Catholics and Puritans.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 3 — Religious matters: the question of religion, English Catholicism and Protestantism; the nature and ideas of the Puritans and Puritanism; Elizabeth and her government's responses and policies towards religious matters.

lessons.title: The Northern Rebellion, excommunication and the missionary threat
lessons.description: The 1569 Northern Rebellion, the 1570 papal excommunication, and the Catholic missionaries who followed.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 3 — the Northern Rebellion; Elizabeth's excommunication; the missionaries; Catholic plots and the threat to the Elizabethan settlement.

lessons.title: Mary, Queen of Scots: plots, trial and execution
lessons.description: Why Mary's flight to England in 1568 ended in plots, the Babington Plot of 1586 and her execution at Fotheringhay.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 3 — Mary Queen of Scots: background; Elizabeth and Parliament's treatment of Mary; the challenge posed by Mary; plots; execution and its impact.

lessons.title: Conflict with Spain and the Spanish Armada (1588)
lessons.description: Why England and Spain went to war, and how the Armada was defeated through tactics, technology and weather.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 3 — Conflict with Spain: reasons; events; naval warfare, including tactics and technology; the defeat of the Spanish Armada.

lessons.title: Living standards, fashion and the rise of the gentry
lessons.description: Why the 'Golden Age' label fits some Elizabethans more than others, and how the gentry rose to prominence.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — A 'Golden Age': living standards and fashions; growing prosperity and the rise of the gentry.

lessons.title: Poverty, vagrancy and the Elizabethan Poor Laws
lessons.description: Why poverty surged in Elizabethan England, why it scared the government, and how the Poor Laws responded.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — The poor: reasons for the increase in poverty; attitudes and responses to poverty; the reasons for government action and the seriousness of the problem.

lessons.title: English sailors: Hawkins, Drake, Raleigh and exploration
lessons.description: Hawkins's slaving voyages, Drake's circumnavigation 1577-1580 and Raleigh's failed colony at Roanoke.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — English sailors: Hawkins and Drake; circumnavigation 1577-1580, voyages and trade; the role of Raleigh.

lessons.title: The Elizabethan theatre and attitudes towards it
lessons.description: Why theatre boomed under Elizabeth, who paid for it, and why Puritans and city authorities pushed back.
lessons.spec_focus: Part 2 — the Elizabethan theatre and its achievements; attitudes to the theatre. Bridges into the Part 4 historic environment site.

thematic_threads: Was this really a 'Golden Age'? Test the label against poverty, religious persecution, the slave-trading voyages of Hawkins, and the failure at Roanoke — not just against theatre, fashion and Drake's gold.
How did Elizabeth survive without an army or a husband? Track court patronage, ministerial talent (Cecil, Walsingham), Parliament management, and image-making (Gloriana, the Armada portrait).

How did religious threat reshape the regime over 35 years? From cautious 1568 settlement, through 1569 Northern Rebellion and 1570 excommunication, to harsh recusancy laws, the execution of Mary in 1587 and war with Spain in 1588.

How does The Globe (the 2026 historic environment site) sit inside all of this? It is the visible artefact of patronage (Lord Chamberlain's Men), of the gentry/middling sort with money to spend, and of the cultural confidence — and the Puritan/civic backlash — that the period produced.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 'Golden Age' as a finding rather than a label invented later. They miss that the same decade gave us Drake's voyages and a sharp rise in vagrancy, harsher recusancy laws and English involvement in the slave trade.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B noting weaker responses to Golden Age questions; History Today, 'Poverty in Elizabethan England'.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Mary Queen of Scots vs Mary I
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students confuse Mary Queen of Scots (Elizabeth's Catholic Stuart cousin, executed 1587) with Mary I (Elizabeth's Tudor half-sister, who died in 1558 before this depth study even begins).
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B Elizabethan questions.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students say the Armada 'was beaten by the weather' and stop there. They miss the role of English fireships at Calais, the lighter and faster English ship design, the breakdown of Spanish supply, and Spanish strategic overreach.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B; Royal Museums Greenwich teaching resources on the Armada.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students assume everyone loved Elizabethan theatre. In fact Puritans, the City of London authorities and many town councils saw playhouses as sites of plague spread, vagrancy, prostitution and disorder, which is why The Globe was built outside the City walls in Southwark.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: Shakespeare's Globe — 'Playhouses' and 'The Globe'; History Today archive on Puritanism and theatre closures.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students describe the site (here The Globe) without ever linking back to the wider events and developments of the period — which is the second-order question prompt the marker is looking for.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B; AQA published answers and commentaries for 8145/2BC.

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students treat 'patronage' as bribery rather than the routine system through which Elizabeth bound nobles, soldiers and even sailors (Drake, Raleigh) to the Crown. Without that, Essex's rebellion in 1601 doesn't make sense — he had just lost his sweet wine monopoly.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: History Today, 'The Fall of Essex' and 'The Execution of the Earl of Essex'.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: The 16-mark historic environment essay must explicitly link the specified site (The Globe in 2026) to wider events and developments of the period — describing the playhouse alone, however accurately, caps the response below the top band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B; AQA answers and commentaries for 8145/2BC.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Top-band responses on Mary Queen of Scots, the Northern Rebellion and the Armada bring in interaction: Mary's existence drove the plots, the plots drove the harsher recusancy laws, the laws drove some Catholics to Spain — leading to the Armada. Lower-band answers treat each event as standalone.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 2 Section B Elizabethan questions; AQA published commentary.

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 8-mark significance question, the strongest answers explain significance both at the time and over time — for example, Drake's circumnavigation mattered in 1580 (knighthood, gold, blow to Spain) and afterwards (English claim to global trade, model for later voyages, Roanoke).
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 significance question across Paper 2 papers.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Sequence the religious thread chronologically across Lessons 5-8 so that students see causation: 1568 settlement → 1569 Northern Rebellion → 1570 excommunication → 1580s plots → 1587 Mary executed → 1588 Armada. Examiner reports show students who learn these as separate topics struggle to write the 8-mark explain question.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 2 Section B Elizabethan; EEF metacognition guidance on modelling causal chains.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Front-load the 'Golden Age' question rather than leaving it to revision. Lesson 9 (rise of gentry/fashion) and Lesson 10 (poverty/Poor Laws) sit deliberately next to each other so students can already weigh evidence on both sides before they see an exam question that asks 'how far'.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — explicit teaching of disciplinary judgement vocabulary; History Today, 'Poverty in Elizabethan England'.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Lesson 12 (theatre and attitudes) is engineered as the bridge into Lesson 13 (The Globe historic environment). Teaching attitudes to the theatre — Puritan opposition, City of London bans, why Bankside was outside city jurisdiction — gives students the wider-period material the 16-marker rewards.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 — historic environment connects site to period; Shakespeare's Globe teaching resources on Bankside playhouses.

pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.note: Cambridge Assessment notes that comparative judgement is the hardest skill at GCSE — schedule retrieval and worked examples on the 16-mark historic environment essay specifically, not just on the 8-mark questions, because students rarely meet that essay format anywhere else in the course.
pedagogical_notes_unit_specific.source: Cambridge Assessment Network and Research, history specifications and reports archive.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Elizabeth I
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Queen of England 1558-1603, central figure of the entire depth study.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Cecil (Lord Burghley)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Elizabeth's principal minister and Lord Treasurer; ran government for almost the whole reign.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Cecil
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William Cecil's son; succeeded him as principal minister; opposed Essex in 1601.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Francis Walsingham
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Principal Secretary and spymaster; uncovered the Babington Plot.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Court favourite turned rebel; led the failed 1601 rebellion; executed for treason.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Catholic Stuart claimant to the English throne; held in England 1568-1587; executed at Fotheringhay.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Francis Drake
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Sea Dog, circumnavigator (1577-1580), vice-admiral against the Armada.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir John Hawkins
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Naval commander, slave trader, redesigner of the English fleet that beat the Armada.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sir Walter Raleigh
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Court favourite and patron of the failed Roanoke colony in North America.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: King Philip II of Spain
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Catholic king who launched the 1588 Armada against England.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pope Pius V
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Issued the 1570 papal bull 'Regnans in Excelsis' excommunicating Elizabeth.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Anthony Babington
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Catholic gentleman whose 1586 plot to free Mary and assassinate Elizabeth led to Mary's execution.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: James Burbage and Richard Burbage
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Father-and-son theatre family; built The Theatre in Shoreditch and then The Globe in Southwark.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Shakespeare
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Playwright and part-owner (sharer) in the Lord Chamberlain's Men at The Globe.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Lord Chamberlain's Men
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Acting company that built and performed at The Globe; patronised by the Lord Chamberlain at court.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Catholic recusants
key_individuals_and_groups.role: English Catholics who refused to attend Anglican services after the 1559 settlement; faced rising fines and persecution from the 1570s.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Puritans
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Hardline Protestants who wanted further reform and were the loudest critics of theatre, fashion and court ritual.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The gentry
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Landowning class below the nobility whose rise reshaped Parliament, county government and fashion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The vagrant poor
key_individuals_and_groups.role: The 'sturdy beggars' and 'impotent poor' whose growing numbers drove the 1572, 1576 and 1598 Poor Laws.

gaps: AQA's published answers and commentaries (8145/2BC) are referenced from the AQA filestore but the specific examiner-quote phrasings could not be transcribed verbatim; the planning brief paraphrases their substance. Content agents should pull live quotes from the published commentary when generating exam-tip blocks.

Lesson 13 covers The Globe as the 2026 historic environment site. Confirmed via aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-history-historic-environment-sites-2026-2028. If a school is using this content for the 2027 or 2028 cycle the site may differ — the lesson title and description must be checked before that year's intake.

Daily life topics in Part 2 of the spec (education, family life beyond fashion, food, music) are folded into Lessons 9 and 12 rather than given a dedicated lesson, in order to keep the historic environment with two lessons of run-up (12 and 13) as the calibration brief recommends. If the agent feels Part 2 daily life is under-covered, Lesson 9 can be widened to include education and household.

content_agent_guardrails_for_he: Do NOT reference the AQA-specified 2026 historic environment site for this option (e.g. Globe, Pevensey, Caernarfon, Ham House). The site rotates yearly and we are deferring that content. Period-general castle/theatre/site content is fine where naturally part of the topic.
